When Moral Grandstanding Replaces Thinking!

Leila de Lima, asserting that because the Philippines is a U.S. ally, Manila supposedly loses its “moral ascendancy” to protest or oppose China’s actions in the SCS, citing U.S. military action against Venezuela as the basis?? Really? Seriously?? 
Let’s be blunt: this is not just wrong. It is conceptually confused, legally incoherent, and geopolitically illiterate. Madam Laila, I think it’s time for you to have more intake of iodized salt; you need some reinforcement. 

Two completely different issues, Madam Laila recklessly conflated.  Her statement collapses two unrelated domains into one sloppy moral syllogism:

• Issue A: The Philippines’ sovereign rights and maritime entitlements in the SCS are grounded in UNCLOS. 

• Issue B: A U.S. military action against Venezuela, which—whatever one thinks of it—is a separate legal and political question involving U.S.–Venezuela relations, not Philippine conduct.

There is no legal doctrine—none—that says a country forfeits its rights under international law because an ally commits a controversial act elsewhere. That is not how international relations work; that is how moral cosplay works.

Second, “Moral ascendancy” in the SCS does not come from who our friends are. It comes from: treaty law (UNCLOS), judicial outcomes, consistent state practice, and documented actions at sea.

Again, I will reiterate, the Philippines’ position in the SCS rests on UNCLOS, not on U.S. global behavior. Suggesting otherwise is legally illiterate, analytically sloppy, and strategically dangerous, as it encourages paralysis rather than principled defense of national interests.

Hence, Madam Laila appears to be suffering from conceptual confusion, raising a serious question about the quality of reasoning expected from lawmakers entrusted with shaping Philippine foreign policy and national discourse. 

Folks, is this the intellectual standard we now accept in the House of Representatives, or from some or most of our lawmakers? Seriously???

Folks, we don’t only have corrupt officials; we apparently also have officials who conflate law with vibes, alliances with absolution, and geopolitics with moral exhibitionism. One is tempted to say some of them need iodized salt, not as an insult, but as a public-health intervention against chronic cognitive deficiency.

Sarcasm aside, Madam Laila’s rhetoric misinforms the public, weakens coherent foreign policy, and trivializes international law—all while pretending to sound principled.

Madam Laila, go on, do criticize U.S. actions in Venezuela if you must. Debate alliance policy if you wish. But don’t insult the intelligence of Filipinos by pretending that defending Philippine maritime rights in the SCS is dependent on U.S. actions, illegitimate or otherwise.

And yes—if this is the level of reasoning by some or most of our legislators shaping national discourse, goodness, we are doomed as a country.
